paragraphs.source_en: These two phases may be compared to the Epipalaeolithic and the Mesolithic phases in the Tassili and Acacus. They also present a continuity of settlement and an economy based exclusively on the exploitation of wild animals and wild plants. In the Adrar Bous the oldest site, Temet I, was dated to 9,550+100 BP (calBP 10,902±169), and in the Air the site of Tagalagal dates to 9,370+130 BP (calBP10, 637±216) (Barich 1998a).

paragraphs.source_en: To the southeast of the Air mountains, on the rim of the Chad Basin, a large cemetery was found in the Gobero plain. There are approximately two hundred human burials on the edge of a palaeo-lake (Sereno et al. 2008). Although the region was frequented by transient hunter-gatherers since at least 16,000 BP, they seem not to have left any burial record. The oldest of these burials dates to around 10,000 BP and belonged to sedentary hunter-fisher-gatherers who abandoned the area for one thousand years during the arid climatic event at around 8,500 BP. After this hiatus other human groups arrived to live and to bury their dead in the same place until around 4,500 BP, showing an outstanding continuity of use for a very long time span, from the 10th millennium BP until the 5th millennium BP.

paragraphs.source_en: The examination of the Gobero skeletons revealed significant differences between the two chronological groups. The first group occupied the site in the Early Holocene until 8,500 BP and were tall and robust, whilst the later group who arrived after the arid phase were smaller and more tiny. This second group who inhabited the site in the Middle Holocene between 7,200 and 4,500 BP utilised domesticated cattle even though hunting and fishing were still largely used (Sereno et al. 2008). This situation has been interpreted as population discontinuity and the same pattern is attested in the Tassili and Acacus sites, where after the Epipalaeolithic and Mesolithic hunter-gatherer occupation new Pastoral population appeared at around 7,500 BP (Aumassip 2004; Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1999).
